title: The Scope Fence Template: Stop Scope Creep Without Losing the Client
description: An in/out scope list, a price list for extras, a change-order form and the "yes, and here's the price" reply. Stop doing free work for clients.
lead: This is the full Scope Fence template from the carousel. Scope creep isn't a client problem, it's a missing fence. This guide gives you the in/out list, a price for every extra, a simple change-order form and the exact reply to send when a client asks for more.
insider: We use the same fence with our own clients: every campaign starts with a written list of what's included (inboxes, lists, copy, follow-ups) and what isn't. That's part of how one agency client of ours got **2,146 interested replies** without the project turning into endless extras. A clear scope keeps both sides happy, and it's how we run every client.

blocks.text: Why scope creep costs so much

In [Ignition's 2025 Agency Pricing and Cash Flow Report](https://www.ignitionapp.com/2025-agency-pricing-cashflow-report) (a survey of 273 US agency leaders), **57% of agencies said they lose $1,000 to $5,000 a month** to unbilled work, and **30% said it costs them more than $5,000 a month**. **78% rarely or only sometimes charge** for out-of-scope work, and only about 1% bill for all of it.
Most of that isn't bad clients. It's small, friendly requests ("can you just...") with no clear line and no price. The fix is a fence: a written line that both sides agreed to before work started.
Step 1: Write what's OUT, not just what's in
Most proposals only list what's included. Clients then assume everything else is included too. Add a second list: what's not included.

head: Included
Not included (priced as extras)
rows: A 3rd or later round of revisions
Copy for new pages, emails or ads

blocks.label: Be specific
blocks.text: "Unlimited revisions" and "ongoing support" are where scope creep starts. Use numbers: 2 rounds, 5 pages, 1 call.
Step 2: Put a price on every extra
When extras already have a price, saying yes is easy and nobody feels awkward. Put a short price list in the contract.
These are examples. Use your own rates, and base each price on the real hours the work takes you.
Step 3: Reply "yes, and here's the price"
Don't say no, and don't do it for free. Say yes, and add the price. You stay helpful, and the client decides.

blocks.label: The reply script
blocks.text:
Happy to do that! 🙌

This one sits outside what we agreed for this month, so it's an extra:
[what they asked for] = $[price], ready by [date].

Want me to go ahead? Just reply "yes" and I'll add it to this month's invoice.
If the request is big, send the change-order form below instead of a quick reply.
Step 4: Bill extras the same month
Extras billed 3 months later feel like a surprise. Add every approved extra to the next invoice, with the date it was approved.
The change-order form

blocks.label: Change-order form (copy it)
blocks.text:
CHANGE ORDER #[number]

Client: [name]
Project: [project]
Date requested: [date]

What's being added:
[describe the extra work in 1-3 lines]

Why it's outside the original scope:
[e.g. new page not in the original 5]

Price: $[amount]
New delivery date: [date]
Effect on other deadlines: [none / moves X by Y days]

Approved by: ______________  Date: ________
Worked example
Say you do 3 extra requests a month, each about 4 hours, at $100 an hour:

items: That's money you were already earning with your time, just not billing.

Doing the extra before it's approved

blocks.text: Make your own fence with Claude

blocks.label: Scope fence prompt
blocks.text:
I run a [type of business] and I sell [service] for $[price] a month.
The client usually gets: [list what you deliver].
Common extra requests I get: [list them].
My hourly rate: $[rate].

Write me:
1) an "Included" and "Not included" list with specific numbers,
2) a price list for the 5 most common extras, based on my hourly rate,
3) a short, friendly "yes, and here's the price" reply I can paste into email or Slack.
Keep it simple and polite.

blocks.label: The rule
blocks.text: It only works if it's signed before kickoff.

faq.q: Won't clients be upset if I charge for extras?
faq.a: Not if it was agreed in writing at the start. Clear prices feel professional. Surprise bills are what upset clients.

faq.q: What if a small request takes 10 minutes?
faq.a: You can do small favors on purpose, but say so: "This one's on us." Then the client knows it's a favor, not part of the deal.

faq.q: I already started the project without a fence. What now?
faq.a: Send the in/out list now as "to keep us both clear going forward", and apply it from next month.
